title: Jonah Runs, and the Sailors Fear the LORD
summary: God sends Jonah to preach against Nineveh, but Jonah boards a ship bound for Tarshish, in the opposite direction. The LORD hurls a violent storm at the sea; the pagan sailors pray, cast lots, and learn that Jonah is fleeing from the God who made the sea. At Jonah's word they throw him overboard, the sea grows calm, and the sailors worship the LORD, while God appoints a great fish to swallow Jonah.
story: Jonah son of Amittai appears once outside this book, in 2 Kings 14:25, as a prophet who foretold that King Jeroboam II would restore Israel's northern border, a prophecy of good news for his own nation. Now the word of the LORD comes to him with a very different assignment: go to Nineveh, a great city of Assyria, the power that would soon threaten and then destroy the northern kingdom. The reader is not told yet why Jonah runs; the book holds that answer back until 4:2. This chapter begins the story's central irony. The prophet who should know God best runs from him, while the outsiders who know nothing of him end up fearing him, praying to him, and offering him sacrifices.
historical:
The story is set in the eighth century BC, during or near the reign of Jeroboam II of Israel (about 793 to 753 BC). Assyria, centered on the upper Tigris in what is now northern Iraq, was the great power of the age and was known for the harsh treatment of peoples it conquered. Nineveh, on the east bank of the Tigris opposite modern Mosul, was one of its principal cities and later became its capital under Sennacherib around 700 BC. It was destroyed by the Babylonians and Medes in 612 BC.

Joppa (modern Jaffa) was a port on the Mediterranean coast, one of the few natural harbors on Israel's shoreline, and it was often under Philistine or Phoenician control. Tarshish lay far to the west; it is often identified with Tartessus in southern Spain, and it stood in the Israelite imagination for the distant edge of the sea (compare Psalm 72:10, Isaiah 66:19). Nineveh was about 500 miles northeast of Israel; Tarshish was more than 2,000 miles west. Jonah chose the farthest destination he could reach.
cultural:
Ancient sailors, often from several nations, each prayed to his own god in a crisis (verse 5), because gods were widely believed to rule particular peoples, lands, or forces of nature. A storm of unusual violence suggested that some god was angry, so the crew cast lots to discover who was responsible (verse 7). Lots were small stones or marked objects drawn or thrown; Israel also used them to discern God's will (Proverbs 16:33, Joshua 7:14-18). The sailors' questions in verse 8 (your occupation, your country, your people) were the natural way to identify which god might be involved.

Jonah's confession in verse 9 terrifies them because he names a God "who made the sea and the dry land". A god of one country could perhaps be escaped by leaving it; a God who made the sea cannot be escaped on the sea. For ancient Near Eastern peoples the sea was also a place of chaos and danger, and a god who stills it is a god above all others. The sailors' reluctance to throw Jonah overboard (verse 13) and their prayer not to be charged with "innocent blood" (verse 14) reflect the widely held belief that bloodguilt brought divine punishment.
literary: The chapter is a masterpiece of storytelling built on repetition. The word "great" (gadol) marks the great city (verse 2), the great wind (verse 4), the sailors' great fear (verses 10 and 16, where the Hebrew says literally they feared a great fear), and the great fish (verse 17). Jonah keeps going "down": down to Joppa, down into the ship, down into its lowest part, and finally down into the sea. The verb "hurl" (tul) is used of God hurling the wind, the sailors hurling cargo, and finally the sailors hurling Jonah. Many scholars see a concentric (chiastic) pattern in the chapter, with Jonah's confession in verse 9 at its center. The sailors' fear grows through three stages, from fear of the storm (verse 5), to great fear at Jonah's confession (verse 10), to fearing the LORD greatly in worship (verse 16). In Hebrew Bibles verse 17 is numbered as 2:1.

outline.t: The call to Nineveh and the flight to Tarshish
The storm, the praying sailors, and the sleeping prophet
The lots fall on Jonah; his confession
Jonah thrown into the sea; the sailors worship the LORD
The LORD appoints a great fish

doctrines.note: The LORD hurls the wind, calms the sea, directs the lot, and appoints the fish. Jonah confesses him as the maker of sea and dry land, and the story shows that no place, not even the open sea, is outside his rule.
God cares about Nineveh's wickedness and sends a prophet to a foreign city. Even Jonah's disobedience becomes an occasion for pagan sailors to come to fear and worship the LORD.

Jonah's sin is flight "away from the presence of the LORD" (verse 3), a phrase repeated for emphasis. The story shows the futility of running from God and the harm that disobedience brings on others, since the sailors nearly perish because of Jonah.

words.note: Tul, to hurl or throw. God hurls a great wind upon the sea (verse 4); the sailors hurl the cargo overboard (verse 5); Jonah tells them to hurl him into the sea, and they do (verses 12 and 15). The repeated verb ties the storm and its solution together: what God hurls is answered when Jonah is hurled.

Yarad, to go down. Jonah goes down to Joppa, down into the ship, and down to its lowest part, and in 2:6 he says he descended to the roots of the mountains. The word traces a downward spiral that mirrors his flight from God, until God himself brings him up.

Yare, to fear. Used for the sailors' terror in the storm and then for their reverent worship of the LORD. The Old Testament often uses the same word for both, and the chapter shows fear of danger turning into the fear of God, the beginning of wisdom (Proverbs 9:10).

Dag, fish. The Hebrew says simply "a great fish", not a whale; the Greek of Matthew 12:40 uses a general word for a sea creature. The text's interest is not in the species but in the fact that God "appointed" it, the first of several things God appoints in the book.

christ: Jesus himself connects this chapter with his own death and resurrection. He said, "For as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the great fish, so the Son of Man will be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth" (Matthew 12:40). Readers have long noticed a striking parallel between this storm and the storm on the Sea of Galilee (Mark 4:35-41), and Mark's wording echoes the Greek of Jonah 1:16: in both a man sleeps in the boat, the sailors wake him in terror, and the sea is calmed, and in both the frightened men end up in greater fear at the power they have seen. But the contrasts are deliberate. Jonah slept because he was running from God; Jesus slept in trust. Jonah had to be thrown into the sea to calm it; Jesus rebuked the wind with a word, and the disciples asked who this was that even the wind and the sea obey him. The answer the book of Jonah gives, the God who made the sea and the dry land, is the answer the Gospels give about Jesus.

hard.q: Why would a prophet try to run away from God, and can anyone really flee his presence?
hard.a: Jonah surely knew the confession of Psalm 139 that no one can escape God's presence. Many interpreters think "away from the presence of the LORD" means away from God's service, as a servant leaves the presence of the king who commands him, or away from the land where the LORD was specially present in his temple. Jonah's reason is held back until 4:2: he knew God was merciful and did not want Nineveh spared. Some readers add patriotic motives, since Assyria threatened Israel, and others suggest Jonah feared being seen as a false prophet if Nineveh were spared. The chapter's point is that flight fails. The God Jonah runs from is the Lord of the sea he runs across.

questions: Jonah ran because he did not want God's mercy to reach people he feared or resented. Is there anyone you would rather God not bless?
The pagan sailors behave more honorably than the prophet. Where have you seen people outside the faith show more integrity than believers, and what should that teach us?
Jonah's disobedience endangered everyone on the ship. How do our private evasions of God affect the people around us?
